A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CPT policy-gradient work despite the changed title. All 33 pages of v1 and 46 pages of v2, including appendices, are readable and support comparison of text, equations, tables, and figures.

before.justification: Section 5 and Appendix F report original grid, traffic-control, electricity-management, batch-size, and policy-class simulations.

after.justification: The original simulations remain, with additional RiskyGridworld, financial-trading, and MuJoCo results in Appendices B and I.

M1.justification: The core CPT-PG estimator, update, and alternative piecewise-weight procedure are retained. Appendix F.7 newly describes an adaptation for non-monotone utilities: sort utility-transformed returns directly when estimating quantiles. This changes a conditional procedure without redesigning the algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 retains the original environments and adds historical BTC-USD trading, InvertedPendulum-v5 continuous control, and a distinct RiskyGridworld scenario involving rare jackpots and penalties. These substantially broaden evaluated domains and conditions. The healthcare example is conceptual.

E2.justification: Appendix B adds an explicit comparison against exponential risk-sensitive policy gradients without probability weighting. The original CPT-SPSA-G scalability comparison and policy-class comparisons remain unchanged. This is a limited comparator addition.

E3.justification: V2 introduces protocols for risky-action heatmaps and separately trained CPT/exponential objectives, trading with 100 episodes, batch size 5 and 25 steps per episode, and control with 2,000 episodes, batch size 32 and a 200-step cap. These are substantial new evaluation settings; retained experiments show no corresponding protocol revision.

E4.justification: Beyond the retained batch-size and Markovian-policy analyses, v2 adds a rare-event policy case study, trading sensitivity to reference point, exponential risk parameter and KT utility curvature, and a curvature comparison in MuJoCo. These substantially expand the behavioral and sensitivity questions examined.

E5.justification: Both versions already use repeated runs, standard-deviation bands, and median/interquartile reporting. Existing experiments retain their stated run counts and conventions. The new trading/control plots extend the existing median/interquartile practice to ten-run results without introducing a new statistical estimation or testing procedure.

E6.justification: The original plotted results are retained. New Figures 5–6 report differing risky-action probabilities and training trajectories; Figures 23–26 add trading and control outcomes across utility settings. These include reference-point shifts and larger reported MuJoCo CPT values with KT alpha 1.4. Different utility objectives prevent interpreting these differences as comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: V2 removes discount factors from the introductory return definition and the relocated occupancy-measure definition, aligning them with the already-undiscounted main CPT objective. The substantive optimal-policy proofs, policy-gradient derivation, and approximation results remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The introduction broadens its critique from expected-utility decision-making to conventional risk-sensitive RL, explicitly claiming limitations in capturing loss asymmetry and probability distortion. Behavioral alignment becomes more prominent, while the central optimal-policy, gradient-theorem, algorithm, and scalability contributions remain.

C2.justification: V2 substantially expands discussion of predefined versus learned preferences, static-preference limitations, RLHF tradeoffs, utility selection, monotonicity, and obstacles to discounted infinite-horizon extensions. It also adds interpretations of rare-event behavior and utility-parameter sensitivity, beyond v1's shorter qualifications.

D1.justification: Appendix B specifies the new policy network, learning rate, and utility/weight parameters. Appendix I.7 documents trading dates, features, actions, rewards, and environment/data access information. Tables 3–4 supply trading and control hyperparameters. These substantially expand reproducibility information; the original hardware and implementation disclosures remain.

R1.justification: V2 adds extensive positioning around CPT applications and preference estimation in healthcare, energy, transport, and finance, plus a substantive comparison with RLHF. It adds works such as Rieger et al. and Hau et al.; the closest CPT-SPSA-G relationship remains. This goes well beyond citation maintenance.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and main experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Section 2 gains a healthcare example and scope discussion; earlier lottery examples move to Appendix F.4, experimental details move into Appendix I, and main-text related work is condensed. The narrative is substantially reorganized.

P2.justification: V2 adds the heatmaps and training plots in Figures 5–6, trading/control Figures 23–26, and hyperparameter Tables 3–4. The scaling-grid panel moves from Figure 1 to standalone Figure 18, while retained displays are resized or relocated. These constitute substantial visual additions and rearrangement.

improvement.justification: The added simulations and concrete settings in Appendices B and I.7–I.8 improve assessment of applicability, while the expanded scope and preference discussions clarify limitations. The gain is limited: the new studies are primarily illustrative, their different utility objectives restrict performance comparisons, and the broad new contrasts with risk-sensitive RL exceed what the single added comparator establishes.
